The case describes a painless, progressive posterior neck swelling over 2 months — a critical topographic clue. “Posterior neck” anatomically corresponds to the **posterior triangle**, which contains the **spinal accessory nerve (CN XI)**, **brachial plexus roots**, **cervical lymph nodes (e.g., supraclavicular, posterior cervical chain)**, and **deep soft tissues including the semispinalis capitis, splenius capitis, and levator scapulae** — but notably *excludes* the thyroid gland (anterior), parotid (lateral/preauricular), submandibular gland (submandibular triangle), and parathyroid glands (deep to thyroid). Among posterior neck masses, the most characteristic *painless, slow-growing, solitary, deep-seated* lesion is a **schwannoma** — a benign nerve sheath tumor, commonly arising from the spinal accessory nerve or dorsal rami of cervical nerves. Schwannomas are typically:  
• Asymptomatic unless large enough to compress adjacent structures;  
• Well-circumscribed, mobile or fixed depending on origin;  
• Radiologically homogeneous with characteristic “target sign” on MRI;  
• Cytologically bland on FNAC (though often nondiagnostic due to paucicellularity);  
• Not associated with systemic findings, lab abnormalities, or serologic triggers.

- Lipoma: Possible, but lipomas are usually *very soft*, compressible, and located in subcutaneous tissue — whereas “posterior neck swelling” without descriptor of consistency suggests deeper origin; also, lipomas rarely prompt such extensive workup unless atypical.  
- Paraganglioma: Typically occurs at carotid bifurcation (anterior triangle) or jugular foramen (not posterior triangle); would be pulsatile/bruit-positive and may secrete catecholamines (not assessed here, but no symptoms suggestive).  
- Sarcoidosis: Granulomatous disease favors bilateral hilar + anterior cervical lymphadenopathy — isolated posterior neck involvement is exceedingly rare.  
- Thyroid/parathyroid: Anatomically implausible — both lie anteriorly.

Thus, the *most specific, location-congruent, behavior-congruent, and test-negative-congruent* diagnosis is **schwannoma**, particularly of the spinal accessory nerve — a classic “posterior triangle mass” in neuro-otolaryngology.

- Painless, progressive posterior neck swelling over 2 months.  
- No pain, tenderness, erythema, or warmth — consistent with benign neural tumor biology.  
- No B symptoms or systemic illness — argues against lymphoma, infection, or granulomatous disease.  
- No palpable lymphadenopathy in axillary, inguinal, or supraclavicular regions — reduces likelihood of disseminated lymphoma or metastatic disease.  
- Normal CBC — compatible with slow-growing benign neoplasm (e.g., schwannoma), unlike aggressive hematologic malignancy.  
- Swelling is localized to posterior neck — anatomically aligned with course of spinal accessory nerve and dorsal cervical nerve roots, common origin of schwannomas.

[GAPS]  
- MRI neck findings (e.g., nerve continuity, target sign, enhancement pattern) — critical to confirm neural origin.  
- FNAC cytology result — though often nondiagnostic for schwannoma, presence of Antoni A/B areas or Verocay bodies would support it.  
- Physical exam details: mobility relative to underlying muscle vs. nerve, transillumination, bruit, neurologic assessment (e.g., shoulder abduction weakness suggesting spinal accessory nerve involvement).  
- Ultrasound characteristics (e.g., hypoechoic, well-defined, longitudinal orientation along nerve).  
- None of the biochemical or serologic tests have reported results — though not expected to be abnormal in schwannoma, their negativity would further narrow differential.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Schwannoma
